title: How money is created: bank credit versus government deficit spending
summary: The speaker says bank loans create credit, not net money: the new deposit and the new loan net to zero in the private sector. Government deficit spending creates net new private-sector assets, because the liability sits with the government, which issues the currency.

steps.caption: This chart is an analogy. Each line shows the net position of the private sector, not a trade.
Bank loan: a new asset (the deposit) and a new liability (the loan). They offset, so the net line is flat at zero.
Deficit spending: the government spends more than it taxes. The private sector gets a new asset with no matching private liability.
The difference is the net new money. The speaker calls bank lending credit creation and deficit spending money creation.
Both drive economic activity. Only the second adds net financial assets to the private sector.

takeaways: Bank lending creates a matching asset and liability in the private sector; the speaker calls it credit creation.
Government deficit spending adds private-sector assets while the liability stays with the government.
A currency-issuing government can always create the liabilities it needs.
caveats: This is a macro opinion lesson with no options trade. The chart uses offsetting positions only as a visual analogy.
The views follow one school of macroeconomics and are not settled consensus.
